newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow backs four-nation talks on Korea.
newsitem.headline: Moscow backs four-nation talks on Korea.

text.p: Russia backs the idea of four-nation talks to work out a lasting peace for the Korean Peninsula but sees other possible options if the talks fail, a senior Russian foreign ministry official said on Monday.

"We support actions, including those in the framework of the so-called "two plus two" formula, aimed at soothing relations between the two parts of Korea," Interfax news agency quoted Deputy Foreign Minister Grigory Karasin as saying.

Karasin was referring to proposed talks to work out a long-term replacement for a now-fraying armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War. The talks would involve North and South Korea as well as the United States and China.
North Korea in April agreed in principle to join the talks but made its participation conditional.

A South Korean Foreign Ministry spokesman said earlier on Monday that Pyongyang was expected to agree to a meeting of senior officials with the United States and South Korea to arrange four-nation peace talks.
Spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung told Reuters officials from the United States and the two Koreas were expected to meet "within the next couple of months" to discuss the agenda for the four-nation talks.
Karasin, who oversees relations with the Far East and Pacific, said that Moscow was ready to take a more active part in Korean talks if the four-nation negotiations failed.

"If this formula runs into difficulties it would be a good time to return to our proposal on widening the format of talks and in fact to start planning an international conference on Korea with the participation of Russia and other interested sides," he said.

Moscow is now negotiating a new basic treaty to shape its relations with Pyongyang, a long time ally of the defunct Soviet Union. Russia and North Korea have agreed that they will no longer be allies and are seeking a balanced treaty to satisfy their interests.

Itar-Tass news agency said Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov met North Korean officials on the first of two days of talks in Moscow. Discussions focused on agreeing the text of a new basic treaty replacing the 1961 Soviet-North Korean pact.
